title: FYP Project
text:
This project automates the monthly reporting workflow for ultra-low temperature freezer units in a facility environment.


Each month, Dickson temperature loggers produce PDF reports for each freezer unit (e.g. S13, S15). Manually extracting and summarising this data was time-consuming and error-prone.



I built a Python-based batch processing pipeline in Jupyter notebooks that:

Reads each Dickson PDF report automatically

Extracts all temperature readings using pypdf

Computes hourly averages and daily statistics

Generates structured Excel workbooks with three sheets:

Readings — raw data with conditional formatting

Hourly Averages — colour-coded by temperature range

Dot Plot — a connected scatter chart (one data point per hour)


Exports PDF versions via LibreOffice

Consolidates all dot plots and hourly averages into combined PDFs





Python — pypdf, openpyxl, pandas

Jupyter Notebooks — for interactive development and batch runs

LibreOffice — headless PDF rendering





Figure: Sample dot plot output for a single freezer unit over one month.

title: Data Visualisation
text:
This visualisation was created as part of my automated facility reporting pipeline. It shows the temperature trends across ultra-low temperature freezer units over a monthly period.


Each freezer unit (e.g. S13, S15) is logged continuously by a Dickson temperature logger. The dot plot below represents hourly average temperatures across the month, colour-coded by severity:



Colour
Temperature Range
Meaning




🔵 Deep Blue
Below −80 °C
Below target — check unit


🔵 Light Blue
−80 °C to −75 °C
Within acceptable range


⬜ White
−75 °C
At target setpoint


🔴 Red
Above −75 °C
Alarm threshold exceeded






Ultra-low freezers store biological samples at around −80 °C. Any sustained deviation above −75 °C risks sample integrity. This visualisation makes it immediately obvious whether a unit had any temperature excursions during the month — without needing to scan through hundreds of raw readings.



The chart is generated programmatically using openpyxl — specifically a 31-series connected scatter chart (one series per day), with exactly two data points per series (start and end of day) to produce a clean dot-plot aesthetic in both Excel and LibreOffice.

Figure: Monthly dot plot for freezer unit S13 — each dot represents an hourly average temperature.




In a well-functioning month, all dots cluster tightly around −80 °C.
Any scatter above −75 °C immediately flags a potential excursion event for investigation.
